chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Abdullah ibn Al-Mughirah, from Al-Hasan ibn Musa Al-Khashshab, from Ali ibn Asbat, from Ibn Abi Layla, from Zurarah, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'My turban fell into urine, so I took it and placed it on my head, then I prayed.' He said, 'There is no harm.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm / It is permissible

ai.seo_question: Is my prayer valid if my clothes were impure but I didn't know?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *al-asl al-suhah* (presumption of original purity) in Shia jurisprudence, where the absence of knowledge regarding impurity (*najis*) does not invalidate the prayer. Imam al-Sadiq’s concise response, 'There is no harm,' underscores that minor, unknown impurities on clothing do not break the validity of the ritual, reflecting the practical leniency applied to everyday worship. This ruling is foundational for understanding how *hadath* and *najis* interact in the context of voluntary acts of devotion.
